title: Indian Americans Win 30 State Legislature Seats Across the United States
excerpt: A post-election tally of 41 tracked candidacies counts 30 wins — every incumbent re-elected, eight winners unopposed, and first-ever Indian-American legislators in Georgia and Texas.
body:
• Indian-American candidates won at least 30 state legislative seats in the November 3 midterms, out of 41 tracked candidacies — 30 wins, two leads and nine losses, according to a tally reported after election night.
  • Every Indian-American incumbent who sought re-election to a state legislature kept their seat, and eight winners ran unopposed; 15 of the winners are women.
  • Firsts included Jyot Singh in Georgia and Pooja Sethi in Texas, each the first Indian American elected to their state legislature.
  • Illinois produced the most winners with four, followed by New York with three; results were still being compiled as the tally was published.

Indian-American candidates won at least 30 state legislative seats in the November 3 midterm elections, the strongest down-ballot showing the community has recorded, according to a post-election tally of 41 tracked candidacies that counted 30 wins, two leads and nine losses. The results, reported by Report Wire on November 5, cap an election in which Democrats took both houses of Congress — covered in our earlier reporting on the midterm results — and Indian-American candidates also won congressional races across the country.

The headline wins

In Michigan, Ranjeev Puri won re-election in the 24th House district with roughly 66 percent of the vote, a result the tally linked to Democrats reclaiming the state house. In Arizona, Priya Sundareshan secured a second term in the 18th district with about 66 percent. Two wins made state history: Jyot Singh won Georgia's 97th House district with nearly 68 percent — 13,800 votes to 6,500 — becoming the first Indian American and first Sikh American elected to the Georgia legislature, and Pooja Sethi won Texas's 47th House district with 63 percent, becoming the first Indian-American woman and first Asian-American Democrat elected to the Texas legislature. Both results were also reported on election night by IANS, which recorded Singh leading by about 68 percent to 32 percent and Sethi declaring victory in District 47.

Incumbents held, and flips landed

Every incumbent who sought re-election retained their seat, according to the tally. Arvind Venkat won re-election in Pennsylvania's House District 30 with 63 percent, and Ram Villivalam retained Illinois Senate District 8 with 73 percent — both also reported by IANS. In Illinois Senate District 26, Nabeela Syed defeated incumbent Darby Hills by 57 percent to 43 percent; IANS had reported her leading by the same margin with more than 95 percent of the estimated vote counted while the race was still uncalled. Other winners in the tally included Anita Somani in Ohio with 71 percent, Saba Haider in Illinois's 84th House district with 71 percent, and Jay Chaudhuri in North Carolina's 15th Senate district with 75 percent. Eight candidates won unopposed, among them Megan Srinivas in Iowa, Nima Kulkarni in Kentucky and Vandana Slatter in Washington.

The pattern in the numbers

Democratic candidates won 28 of 33 declared races in the tally, an 85 percent success rate, and 15 of the 30 winners are women. Illinois produced the most winners with four, followed by New York with three, and Washington and Vermont with two each. Republican wins in the tally included Sabi Kumar holding Tennessee's 66th House district with 66 percent. The state results sat alongside higher-profile outcomes the same night: Aruna Miller was re-elected as Maryland's lieutenant governor on Governor Wes Moore's ticket, while Vivek Ramaswamy lost the Ohio governor's race to Democrat Amy Acton, IANS reported.

What to watch

The tally was compiled while complete local-level results were still being gathered, and two tracked candidates were listed as leading rather than declared winners, so the final count could still move. What is already clear is the depth of the bench: with 30 legislators spread across state houses from Georgia to Washington, Indian-American representation in American politics now rests as much on state capitols as on the smaller group in Congress — the arena where redistricting, election rules and much of education and health policy are actually decided.
